title: Cage-Free Eggs May Have Worse Environmental Impact
paragraphs: In many countries, consumers, retailers and governments have been moving away from eggs produced by hens kept in cages, mainly because of concerns about animal welfare. However, a new study suggests that this shift may come with an unexpected environmental cost.

The study, titled "The environmental cost of welfare-driven policy," was published on July 29, 2026, in the journal Royal Society Open Science. Its lead author is Oliver Martinić, an independent researcher based in Croatia, and his co-author is Dr. Harriet Bartlett of the Oxford Martin Programme on the Future of Food at the University of Oxford.

Using data on laying hens in the UK, the researchers compared several scenarios for the egg industry, including shifts to barn, free-range and organic systems, while keeping the total number of eggs produced the same. According to their calculations, moving entirely to free-range and organic production would increase greenhouse gas emissions by around 60% and nearly double the amount of land used.

The main reason is efficiency. Hens in caged systems convert feed into eggs more efficiently, so fewer birds are needed to produce the same number of eggs. Organic free-range systems had the highest emissions and pollution, because the hens are less productive, eat more feed per egg and depend on organic crops, which produce lower yields. In addition, the death rate among hens rose significantly in fully free-range and organic systems. This is due to greater exposure to disease, predators, injuries and feather pecking, and birds that die consume resources without producing eggs.

Importantly, the authors do not recommend a return to cages, and they recognize that cage-free systems are important for animal welfare. Instead, they argue that farms need to reduce mortality and improve feed efficiency through better genetics, nutrition and management. "Being aware of these tricky trade-offs will help us make better decisions," Bartlett said.

The study also has limitations. Its data were collected in 2009 and 2010, so they do not reflect improvements made since then. Martinić said, however, that these data remain the most comprehensive available for all UK systems. Furthermore, mortality is only one measure of welfare and does not capture the animals' behavior or emotional well-being.
